Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says there will be no fall legislative session as the new Conservative government gets its bearings in the short window between being sworn in and the holiday season. “Our government has an ambitious agenda, and we want to ensure legislation is properly prepared and receives the debate and consideration it deserves,” Doerkson said in a written statement on Monday (Nov. 16). The B.C. Conservative Party will have a large majority in the legislature when it does convene, after the party won 64 of 93 seats in the Oct. 24 election. Doerkson had left the door open to recalling the legislature for a short session before the end of the year as he seeks to pursue a slate of changes after nine years of NDP government. Conservative MLAs are scheduled to be sworn in on Thursday evening. The premier and cabinet will then be sworn in on Friday, officially taking the reins of the B.C. government. “Ministers will get to work from day one, advancing our priorities and preparing a substantive legislative agenda for the spring,” Doerkson said. The incoming government can accomplish a lot simply by taking administrative control of the various government ministries and by issuing cabinet orders. This could include changes to the Massey Tunnel project. Doerkson has promised to scrap the tunnel and build a bridge instead. The new government could also get started building other infrastructure, like the promised urgent care centres and Surrey women’s and children’s hospital. Other major campaign promises will need to wait, like the promised repeal of the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, or alterations to B.C.’s no-fault car insurance rules. These will require legislation.

Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data; they started giving us inconsistency in the data … and because of that we shut the system down.” ​The ground stop did not come from a threat to the United States and was not linked to this week’s Microsoft outage, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullen. ​Travel impacts could last several days while airports and airlines comb through thousands of cancellations and delays.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Federal memo warns freshwater pressures threaten Canada’s long-term security
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

items.title: [ft.com] Milburn review urges youth hiring tax cuts and benefit overhaul
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Former Labour minister Alan Milburn’s youth-employment review, due Tuesday, is expected to urge the government to phase in a higher employer National Insurance threshold for workers aged 21 to 24, tighten some benefits and guarantee young people work, training or employment support. The review addresses the nearly one million people aged 16 to 24 who are not in education, employment or training. items.title: [theguardian.com] UN warns climate adaptation funding leaves vulnerable countries exposed
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report says developing countries remain exposed to worsening floods, droughts and heat because adaptation funding is not reaching vulnerable communities at the scale required. Least-developed countries and small island states need an estimated $40 billion to $50 billion annually, equivalent to 3% to 4% of their gross domestic product, while support to least-developed countries fell 16% from 2022 to 2024. Adaptation measures include flood barriers, heat-resistant hospitals and drought-resilient water and farming systems. Low- and middle-income countries accounted for 99% of the 765 million people affected by floods and landslides between 2020 and 2025. Communities also face obstacles to turning plans into projects, including weak institutional coordination and difficulty accessing funding for climate-related losses. At the COP31 climate conference, opening in Antalya on Nov. 9, campaigners are urging governments to set out a concrete funding plan and prioritize grants or concessional loans over high-interest borrowing for projects that generate little direct revenue. Concessional loans are easier to repay than high-interest loans.

items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

Their application, filed on Friday, Nov. 6, challenges both the High Court’s rejection of the claims and a later order on the publisher’s legal costs. The claimants alleged that journalists or people working for the publisher used unlawful information-gathering methods, including voicemail interception and deception; Associated Newspapers denied the allegations. After an 11-week trial, High Court judge Matthew Nicklin ruled on July 7 that none of the seven claimants had proved unlawful information gathering. He accepted journalists’ explanations that the articles came from lawful sources and said suspicion alone could not establish the claims. The claimants say the rulings are “legally and factually flawed”. In August, Nicklin ordered an initial payment of £9,544,355 toward the publisher’s costs, with the final amount to be determined at a separate hearing. He ordered costs to be assessed on an indemnity basis, which can allow greater recovery. Associated Newspapers estimated its defence costs at about £34.5 million by July 9. The Court of Appeal must first decide whether to grant permission to appeal.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN warns 2026 heat records signal accelerating climate extremes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Earth’s energy imbalance has reached its highest level since monitoring began, and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Global surface temperature averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level from January through September; a developing, unusually strong El Niño could push the annual figure higher and prolong extreme heat into 2027. The agency released its report as the U.N. climate summit COP31 opened in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiations scheduled through Nov. 20. The agency says each of the past 12 years ranked among the 12 warmest on record, with 2023-2026 likely to be the four warmest years. Greenhouse gases from human activity are trapping heat; the ocean absorbs about 90% of the excess, while sea levels and ocean temperatures have reached records. The WMO warns that the accumulating heat will intensify heat waves, droughts, tropical cyclones and heavy rain. A separate U.N. Environment Programme assessment says warming will exceed 1.5°C under every plausible emissions pathway. Returning below that threshold this century would require near-zero emissions and the removal of hundreds of billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide. The WMO’s full 2026 climate report is due in March 2027.

items.content_html:

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

items.title: [elpais.com] Cyberattacks on refrigeration systems fuel concerns about connected household appliances
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Cyberattacks on internet-connected refrigeration systems in supermarkets and French blood banks have destroyed food in Europe and heightened concerns about connected devices. Nearly 800 freezers were sabotaged in France and Northern Europe this week. On November 2, temperatures also rose in the cold rooms of a blood donation service in France. There, alarms and swift action prevented damage to stored blood. The targeted systems used internet-accessible controls for maintenance and remote operation. According to experts, similar attacks on private smart-home devices are less likely because, with typical router configurations, the devices cannot be accessed directly from the internet. Risks include outdated software, weak passwords, and devices with cameras or microphones. Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security recommends automatic updates, separate networks for smart-home devices, and unique passwords. The identity of those behind the attacks remains unclear.

The agency did not say who carried out the attacks. Moscow-appointed plant management blamed Ukrainian forces for the nuclear-plant worker’s death, while Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly accused each other of attacks around the site. The nuclear plant’s six reactors have been shut down since 2022, but safety systems still require electricity. On Nov. 8, the plant lost its sole 330-kilovolt external power line for about 10 hours and used emergency diesel generators for cooling and other safety functions until power returned. The IAEA has maintained a presence at the facility since September 2022. The latest deaths followed the reported killing of another plant employee in a drone attack on Oct. 29. IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi condemned the attacks and called for them to stop. The agency has not publicly assigned responsibility for the strikes.

items.title: [europapress.es] Spain, Netherlands nominate rivals to succeed ECB chief Christine Lagarde
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Spain and the Netherlands have formally nominated former central-bank chiefs Pablo Hernández de Cos and Klaas Knot as the only candidates to replace European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde, who plans to leave on Feb. 7, 2027, before her term ends. Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis confirmed the two names after the Nov. 6 deadline. Euro-area finance ministers will discuss the candidates on Nov. 9 but are not expected to choose a winner then. Hernández de Cos, now director general of the Bank for International Settlements, led the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024. Knot led the Dutch central bank from 2011 to 2025 and chaired the Financial Stability Board from 2021 to 2025. The ECB sets euro-area interest rates and aims to keep prices stable. The appointment is part of negotiations over three senior ECB roles: the presidency, the executive-board seat Isabel Schnabel is expected to leave in January to join the International Monetary Fund, and the post of chief economist Philip Lane, whose term ends in May 2027. EU leaders make the final choice after consultations with the European Parliament and the ECB. They are expected to discuss the succession at meetings later in November and December.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] India’s opposition demands poll chief’s resignation over voter-roll cuts
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Tens of thousands of people gathered at New Delhi’s Ramlila Maidan on Sunday for a rally by the opposition INDIA bloc, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a nationwide voter-roll revision. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi led a march to the venue, where the opposition accused the Election Commission of removing eligible voters from the rolls. The commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) deny wrongdoing. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which began last year, removed about 130 million names from draft electoral rolls. Opposition parties say the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim and other minority voters and could benefit the BJP. The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove entries for people who have died or moved, as well as duplicate entries. The rally followed a symbolic opposition “impeachment” of Kumar on Saturday that carries no legal force. The commission says voters wrongly removed from the rolls can re-enrol. Under India’s constitution, removing the chief election commissioner requires a formal parliamentary process and a special majority.

items.title: [cnbc.com] France-led protests spread to 31 European countries as rallies continue
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

France’s protest movement over living costs, wages and public services has spread to 30 other European countries, with more than 1,700 demonstrations recorded across the continent from Sept. 15 to Oct. 30, according to an analysis of Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) figures. In France, the protests began with students challenging school conditions and widened to include unions and other groups. On Saturday, Nov. 7, the Interior Ministry counted 146,000 demonstrators nationwide, including 46,000 in Paris; unions estimated 250,000 and 75,000, respectively. It was the fourth consecutive Saturday of protests, and clashes followed in Paris and other cities. French authorities deployed about 70,000 security personnel on Saturday. The Interior Ministry recorded at least 360 arrests nationwide, according to AFP. Attendance was down from earlier weekends and from Thursday’s union rally, which drew 575,000 people by the government’s count. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to meet labor unions and employer representatives on Monday, Nov. 9, to discuss wages and purchasing power. Student and teacher groups have called for a strike on Tuesday, while France’s Senate is scheduled to begin debating the government’s 2027 budget proposal on Nov. 20.

A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the ship’s stern after the crew was told to leave the targeted areas. The U.S. military did not provide details on the crew’s condition or damage to the vessel. The U.S. also announced a task force to disrupt Iranian transfers of advanced weapons, sanctioned goods and other materials overland and through the Caspian Sea, in addition to its months-long naval blockade. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) says the blockade has prevented more than $25 billion in Iranian crude-oil exports. On Nov. 8, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines in the Strait of Hormuz while using unauthorized routes. Separately, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) said it rescued 22 crew members from a burning cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman. It was unclear whether that ship was the Huda or another vessel.

Peru declared an emergency across more than 70% of its municipalities over flood danger, with authorities warning that more than 9 million people face a high risk of floods and landslides. In the Philippines, unmilled rice production fell 18% in the three months to September, while forecasters expect below-normal rainfall in November. Nearly 896,000 hectares have burned in Indonesia since January; smoke has led to school closures and respiratory illness, according to a report citing BBC. Cereal maker Kellanova has also changed the ingredients in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops sold in the UK and Europe, citing weather-related problems with the availability and quality of rice and grains. The UN’s International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) says overlapping climate and economic shocks could cost the global economy as much as $11 trillion, with energy and fertilizer costs adding pressure across food systems. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said in September it had received only one-fifth of the $202 million requested to prepare for food crises in 22 high-risk countries.

items.title: [theeastafrican.co.ke] Somali court orders election within 90 days as EAC urged to mediate
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Somalia’s Supreme Court invalidated extensions to the president’s and parliament’s terms but left constitutional amendments in place, giving politicians 90 days to arrange an election and agree on an electoral model. The ruling did not resolve the dispute between President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s government and its opponents over the amendments and election rules. The East African Community (EAC), the regional bloc Somalia joined in 2023, is being urged to help mediate as the African Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) and other partners grow weary of the dispute. Uganda has begun withdrawing troops from Somalia in phases; Mohamud met Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni on Oct. 26 to seek an extension of their deployment. Somalia’s government has invited opposition groups to talks in Mogadishu from Nov. 14 to 18, but major coalitions had not confirmed attendance.
